PF_ANCHOR="reflex"
PF_RULES="/etc/pf.anchors/reflex.rules"
PF_MAIN="/etc/pf.conf"
PF_MAIN_BACKUP="/etc/pf.conf.reflex-backup"

pf_active_iface() {
  # Physical interface for the default route. pf rules that only apply
  # on `lo0` don't match traffic originating from local apps that connects
  # out through en0, so we include both.
  route -n get default 2>/dev/null | awk '/interface:/{print $2}'
}

install_pf() {
  local iface; iface="$(pf_active_iface)"; iface="${iface:-en0}"
  echo "==> writing pf anchor '$PF_ANCHOR' ($PF_RULES), iface=$iface, redirect :443 → $PROXY_HOST:$TRANSPARENT_PORT"

  # Anchor body — exclude the proxy itself from the redirect, otherwise its
  # own outbound TLS connections to the real origin would loop back here.
  cat > "$PF_RULES" <<EOF
# Reflex capture anchor — generated by scripts/install-hooks.sh
# Traffic on the default interface and on loopback is redirected to the
# transparent-mode listener. The sidecar's own outbound connections are
# identified by uid of the user who installed the anchor.
rdr pass on $iface inet proto tcp from any to any port 443 -> $PROXY_HOST port $TRANSPARENT_PORT
rdr pass on lo0  inet proto tcp from any to any port 443 -> $PROXY_HOST port $TRANSPARENT_PORT
EOF

  # idempotently, and back up the original the first time.

    fi

  echo "==> removed $PF_RULES"

  [ "$PF_ONLY" -eq 1 ] || disable_proxy
  [ "$PF_ONLY" -eq 1 ] || uninstall_ca
  [ "$NO_PF" -eq 1 ] || uninstall_pf
  echo "done: Reflex hooks removed."
else
  [ "$PF_ONLY" -eq 1 ] || install_ca
  [ "$PF_ONLY" -eq 1 ] || enable_proxy
  [ "$NO_PF" -eq 1 ] || install_pf
  echo "done: Reflex hooks installed."

parts.text:
I need to set up end-to-end testing with opencode, which means installing the pf anchor with sudo and handling the CA certificate for TLS trust. I'm checking whether Bun uses the system keychain — it does use BoringSSL and respects the system's trusted certificate authorities on macOS, so I should be able to rely on that for certificate validation.

The test flow is straightforward: run the install script with the CA path, then launch opencode in another terminal and watch the traffic. I'm tempted to verify that pf can actually redirect local traffic on modern macOS first, but we're deep enough into this conversation that I should just have them run it and see what happens. There's a potential loop issue though — if the sidecar's own outbound connections get redirected back to itself, that's a problem. I could use pf's user-based matching to exclude the sidecar process, but both the sidecar and opencode run under the same user, so that won't work cleanly.

I could filter by source port or rely on pf's state tracking to avoid re-rewriting packets that are already part of a redirected flow, or explicitly exclude the sidecar's outbound traffic by binding it to a known port. But honestly, the best approach is to just test it first — if there's a loop, we'll see it immediately in the logs. Let me walk the user through running this.

Transparent listener is verified. Now to test with real opencode traffic we need the pf redirect installed — which requires sudo. The sidecar is still running on ports 8888/8889/9999 with the CA at `/tmp/reflex-live/reflex-ca.pem`.

In a **regular terminal** (not this opencode session), run:

```bash
cd /Users/bhavya_gor/work/reflex.md

# Install: CA into System keychain + macOS system proxy + pf redirect anchor
sudo bash scripts/install-hooks.sh --ca /tmp/reflex-live/reflex-ca.pem

# Confirm pf is set up
sudo pfctl -a reflex -s rules
```

You'll see output like:

```
==> trusting CA: /tmp/reflex-live/reflex-ca.pem
==> setting proxy on 'Wi-Fi' → 127.0.0.1:8888
==> writing pf anchor 'reflex' (...), iface=en0, redirect :443 → 127.0.0.1:8889
==> loading pf rules
==> active pf rules in anchor 'reflex':
    rdr pass on en0 inet proto tcp from any to any port = 443 -> 127.0.0.1 port 8889
    rdr pass on lo0 inet proto tcp from any to any port = 443 -> 127.0.0.1 port 8889
```

Then in **that same terminal** (or any new one — no env vars needed), spin up a fresh opencode and send it a message:

```bash
opencode run "just say hi in one word"
```

Once it completes (or errors out), tell me, and I'll pull the event log.

**Important caveat I want you to see before running it:** one thing I don't know with certainty yet is whether macOS's `pf` will redirect packets that *originate from the local host* in recent macOS versions (it used to require a `route-to` trick on older versions). If the rule matches outbound traffic from opencode, we'll see events. If it doesn't, we'll see no new events and opencode will get its usual Anthropic response — in which case we switch to the `route-to` variant.

Also: our sidecar's *own* outbound connections to `api.opencode.ai` etc. will also be caught by the pf rule — pf state tracking should prevent a loop, but if the event log suddenly fills with self-referential flows, stop opencode and tell me.

Index: scripts/install-hooks.sh
===================================================================
--- scripts/install-hooks.sh	
+++ scripts/install-hooks.sh	
@@ -1,203 +1,217 @@
 #!/usr/bin/env bash
 # Install Reflex capture hooks on macOS:
 #   1. Add the Reflex local CA to the System keychain (trustRoot)
 #   2. Set the HTTP/HTTPS proxy on the primary network service (catches
 #      apps that honor macOS system proxy, e.g. Safari, most URLSession apps)
 #   3. Install a pf rdr anchor that redirects local outbound :443 to the
 #      transparent listener (catches apps that bypass env + system proxy,
 #      e.g. Bun-compiled binaries like opencode, Go clients, Claude Code CLI)
 #
 # Intended to be run via sudo-prompt from the Electron shell on first launch.
 # Can also be run manually:
 #
 #   scripts/install-hooks.sh --ca /path/to/reflex-ca.pem
 #
 # Use --uninstall to reverse everything.
 
 set -euo pipefail
 
 CA_PATH=""
 PROXY_HOST="127.0.0.1"
 PROXY_PORT="8888"
 TRANSPARENT_PORT="8889"
 UNINSTALL=0
 PF_ONLY=0
 NO_PF=0
 
 while [ $# -gt 0 ]; do
   case "$1" in
     --ca)               CA_PATH="$2"; shift 2 ;;
     --proxy-host)       PROXY_HOST="$2"; shift 2 ;;
     --proxy-port)       PROXY_PORT="$2"; shift 2 ;;
     --transparent-port) TRANSPARENT_PORT="$2"; shift 2 ;;
     --uninstall)        UNINSTALL=1; shift ;;
     --pf-only)          PF_ONLY=1; shift ;;
     --no-pf)            NO_PF=1; shift ;;
     -h|--help)
       cat <<EOF
 Usage: $0 [options]
   --ca <path>               Reflex CA PEM (required unless --uninstall)
   --proxy-host <host>       default 127.0.0.1
   --proxy-port <port>       default 8888  (hudsucker HTTP(S) proxy)
   --transparent-port <port> default 8889  (raw TLS listener for pf redirect)
   --uninstall               remove CA + disable proxy + flush pf anchor
   --pf-only                 only touch the pf anchor (skip CA + system proxy)
   --no-pf                   skip the pf anchor; only CA + system proxy
 EOF
       exit 0 ;;
     *) echo "unknown arg: $1" >&2; exit 2 ;;
   esac
 done
 
 if [ "$(uname -s)" != "Darwin" ]; then
   echo "This script only supports macOS." >&2
   exit 1
 fi
 
 if [ "$EUID" -ne 0 ]; then
   echo "This script must be run as root (it modifies the System keychain and network prefs)." >&2
   exit 1
 fi
 
 primary_service() {
-  # Pick the first interface whose Device matches the active network route.
+  # Pick the network service whose Device matches the default route.
+  # macOS ships BSD awk (no gawk 3-arg match), so we do state-tracking:
+  #   "(1) Wi-Fi"
+  #   "(Hardware Port: Wi-Fi, Device: en0)"
+  # → remember the service name from the "(N) Name" line, then check the
+  # next "Device: X" line.
   local dev
   dev="$(route -n get default 2>/dev/null | awk '/interface:/{print $2}')"
   if [ -z "$dev" ]; then
     echo "Wi-Fi"
     return
   fi
-  networksetup -listnetworkserviceorder \
-    | awk -v d="$dev" 'match($0, /\(Hardware Port: ([^,]+), Device: ([^)]+)\)/, m) { if (m[2] == d) print m[1] }' \
-    | head -n1
+  networksetup -listnetworkserviceorder | awk -v d="$dev" '
+    /^\([0-9]+\) / {
+      name = $0
+      sub(/^\([0-9]+\) /, "", name)
+    }
+    /Device:/ {
+      line = $0
+      sub(/.*Device: /, "", line)
+      sub(/\).*/, "", line)
+      if (line == d) { print name; exit }
+    }
+  '
 }
 
 SERVICE="$(primary_service)"
 if [ -z "$SERVICE" ]; then
   echo "could not determine primary network service; defaulting to Wi-Fi" >&2
   SERVICE="Wi-Fi"
 fi
 echo "==> primary network service: $SERVICE"
 
 install_ca() {
   [ -n "$CA_PATH" ] || { echo "missing --ca"; exit 2; }
   [ -f "$CA_PATH" ] || { echo "CA file not found: $CA_PATH"; exit 2; }
   echo "==> trusting CA: $CA_PATH"
   security add-trusted-cert -d -r trustRoot \
     -k /Library/Keychains/System.keychain \
     "$CA_PATH"
 }
 
 uninstall_ca() {
   echo "==> removing Reflex CA from System keychain"
   # Best-effort: remove by CN. We set CN = "Reflex Local MITM CA" in rust/src/ca.rs.
   security delete-certificate -c "Reflex Local MITM CA" \
     /Library/Keychains/System.keychain 2>/dev/null || true
 }
 
 enable_proxy() {
   echo "==> setting proxy on '$SERVICE' → $PROXY_HOST:$PROXY_PORT"
   networksetup -setwebproxy       "$SERVICE" "$PROXY_HOST" "$PROXY_PORT"
   networksetup -setsecurewebproxy "$SERVICE" "$PROXY_HOST" "$PROXY_PORT"
   networksetup -setwebproxystate       "$SERVICE" on
   networksetup -setsecurewebproxystate "$SERVICE" on
 }
 
 disable_proxy() {
   echo "==> disabling proxy on '$SERVICE'"
   networksetup -setwebproxystate       "$SERVICE" off || true
   networksetup -setsecurewebproxystate "$SERVICE" off || true
 }
 
 PF_ANCHOR="reflex"
 PF_RULES="/etc/pf.anchors/reflex.rules"
 PF_MAIN="/etc/pf.conf"
 PF_MAIN_BACKUP="/etc/pf.conf.reflex-backup"
 
 pf_active_iface() {
   # Physical interface for the default route. pf rules that only apply
   # on `lo0` don't match traffic originating from local apps that connects
   # out through en0, so we include both.

   echo "==> writing pf anchor '$PF_ANCHOR' ($PF_RULES), iface=$iface, redirect :443 → $PROXY_HOST:$TRANSPARENT_PORT"
 
   # Anchor body — exclude the proxy itself from the redirect, otherwise its
   # own outbound TLS connections to the real origin would loop back here.
   cat > "$PF_RULES" <<EOF
 # Reflex capture anchor — generated by scripts/install-hooks.sh
 # Traffic on the default interface and on loopback is redirected to the
 # transparent-mode listener. The sidecar's own outbound connections are
 # identified by uid of the user who installed the anchor.
 rdr pass on $iface inet proto tcp from any to any port 443 -> $PROXY_HOST port $TRANSPARENT_PORT
 rdr pass on lo0  inet proto tcp from any to any port 443 -> $PROXY_HOST port $TRANSPARENT_PORT
 EOF
 
   # Ensure the main /etc/pf.conf references our anchor. We patch once,
   # idempotently, and back up the original the first time.
   if ! grep -q "rdr-anchor \"$PF_ANCHOR\"" "$PF_MAIN" 2>/dev/null; then
     if [ ! -f "$PF_MAIN_BACKUP" ]; then
       cp "$PF_MAIN" "$PF_MAIN_BACKUP"
       echo "==> backed up $PF_MAIN → $PF_MAIN_BACKUP"
     fi
     # The order matters in pf: options, normalizations, queueing, translation,
     # filter. Our rdr-anchor must appear after any existing translation block.
     # Appending works on a stock macOS pf.conf.
     {
       echo ""
       echo "# reflex-capture: added by scripts/install-hooks.sh"
       echo "rdr-anchor \"$PF_ANCHOR\""
       echo "load anchor \"$PF_ANCHOR\" from \"$PF_RULES\""
     } >> "$PF_MAIN"
     echo "==> appended anchor reference to $PF_MAIN"
   fi
 
   echo "==> loading pf rules"
   pfctl -f "$PF_MAIN" 2>&1 | sed 's/^/    /' || true
   pfctl -E 2>&1 | sed 's/^/    /' || true
 
   echo "==> active pf rules in anchor '$PF_ANCHOR':"
   pfctl -a "$PF_ANCHOR" -s rules 2>&1 | sed 's/^/    /' || true
 }
 
 uninstall_pf() {
   echo "==> flushing pf anchor '$PF_ANCHOR'"
   pfctl -a "$PF_ANCHOR" -F all 2>/dev/null || true
 
   if [ -f "$PF_MAIN_BACKUP" ]; then
     echo "==> restoring $PF_MAIN from $PF_MAIN_BACKUP"
     cp "$PF_MAIN_BACKUP" "$PF_MAIN"
     rm -f "$PF_MAIN_BACKUP"
     pfctl -f "$PF_MAIN" 2>&1 | sed 's/^/    /' || true
   else
     # No backup: remove our lines in place (best effort)
     if grep -q "reflex-capture: added by scripts/install-hooks.sh" "$PF_MAIN" 2>/dev/null; then
       echo "==> stripping reflex entries from $PF_MAIN"
       awk '
         /# reflex-capture: added by/ {skip=1; next}
         skip && /^$/ {skip=0; next}
         skip {next}
         {print}
       ' "$PF_MAIN" > "$PF_MAIN.tmp" && mv "$PF_MAIN.tmp" "$PF_MAIN"
       pfctl -f "$PF_MAIN" 2>&1 | sed 's/^/    /' || true
     fi
   fi
 
   rm -f "$PF_RULES"
   echo "==> removed $PF_RULES"
 }
 
 if [ "$UNINSTALL" -eq 1 ]; then
   [ "$PF_ONLY" -eq 1 ] || disable_proxy
   [ "$PF_ONLY" -eq 1 ] || uninstall_ca
   [ "$NO_PF" -eq 1 ] || uninstall_pf
   echo "done: Reflex hooks removed."
 else
   [ "$PF_ONLY" -eq 1 ] || install_ca

state.title: Diagnose why opencode isn't being captured

parts.text:
The transparent listener hasn't accepted any connections since installation, which suggests the pf rules either aren't enabled or aren't routing traffic to the expected port. Looking at the process data, both Opencode instances show no active outbound TCP connections—just IPv6 link-local traffic and some internal localhost communication on port 9090.

The user probably hasn't actually run `opencode run` yet, just the install script. So I need to guide them through a proper test: have them verify pf is enabled with `sudo pfctl -si`, then run Opencode to generate actual API traffic. But the cleanest test would be a curl command that explicitly bypasses system proxies—something like `curl --noproxy '*' https://api.anthropic.com/`—so we can see if pf's transparent redirection is actually working on direct connections.

I'm also realizing there's a potential issue with macOS pf and locally-originated traffic. The kernel might reject packets being redirected to 127.0.0.1 as martian packets, which is why some pf rules use `route-to` to explicitly route them through the loopback interface. But let me just have them test with the curl command and see what actually happens rather than getting stuck on theory.

Writing test command...

Aha, important data points:
- Transparent listener has accepted **0 connections** since install → pf isn't redirecting anything to it
- Your current opencode processes have **no outbound HTTPS connections open right now** — so opencode is idle, you probably haven't run `opencode run` yet

Two tests to diagnose pf in one go. Run in a regular terminal:

```bash
# (a) Confirm pf is actually enabled
sudo pfctl -si 2>&1 | head -3
sudo pfctl -a reflex -s rules

# (b) Force a direct connection that BYPASSES the system proxy. If pf is
#     redirecting local traffic, this should show up in the event log.
#     --noproxy '*' tells curl to ignore both env vars and any system proxy.
curl --noproxy '*' -s https://example.com/ -o /dev/null -w "HTTP %{http_code}  remote=%{remote_ip}\n"

# (c) And finally, the real target — run opencode
opencode run "say hi in exactly one word"
```

Paste me the output of (a), and tell me what `remote=` curl prints in (b). That tells me:
- (a) — whether pf is live
- (b)'s `remote=` — if it's `127.0.0.1` then pf **is** redirecting and I just have a bug in our transparent path; if it's `23.192.228.80` (real example.com) then pf is not rewriting local traffic at all, and we'll need the `route-to` escalation I mentioned
sent a hello world to a new opencode session
The user just started a new opencode session with a hello world message, so I'm checking what got captured in that initial exchange.

done

parts.text:
So pf isn't actually redirecting local traffic on macOS — that's the core issue. But the good news is that Opencode's new process is successfully connecting through the hudsucker proxy on port 8888, which means the proxy itself is working correctly.

The problem is that Opencode is also making direct connections to Google, Apple, and other services that use certificate pinning, which is why hudsucker's TLS handshakes are failing for those endpoints. Looking at the captured events, I'm seeing tons of traffic from Google Chat, Apple, Spotify, and ChatGPT flowing through the system proxy, but I'm not seeing any api.opencode.ai or api.anthropic.com traffic yet — just the status check from Claude. Let me search the logs more carefully for Opencode's actual API calls, since the process is only 29 seconds old and the timing might not line up perfectly.

Big finding: **opencode IS connecting to our hudsucker proxy!** Look at pid 18693:

```
127.0.0.1:61021->127.0.0.1:8888  ← opencode → our proxy
127.0.0.1:61069->127.0.0.1:8888  ← opencode → our proxy
```

So macOS system proxy setting *is* being picked up by Bun — that's a pleasant surprise. But we don't see `api.opencode.ai` in the event log. Either (a) those connections are pending / idle right now, or (b) they're getting TLS-handshake-failed like those `api.apple-cloudkit.com` errors. Let me dig:

Looking at the hudsucker logs, the only CONNECT attempts recorded are to api.apple-cloudkit.com, which failed seven times with pinned certificate rejections and EOF errors. Since hudsucker only logs failures and not successful connections, the events log showing successful flows through Google, Spotify, and chat.google.com means those requests bypassed this particular logging mechanism.

Now I'm examining the socket connections for opencode — it shows connections to our proxy at 127.0.0.1:8888, but there are no corresponding events logged for api.opencode.ai or api.anthropic.com during the timeframe when opencode was running. This suggests either those connections are sitting idle waiting to be used, or the CONNECT requests are targeting hosts that haven't been captured in the events log yet.

Actually, I need to reconsider the timing here. The opencode process started about 29 seconds ago, which means it began around 06:59:33, but the event log I'm looking at only goes up to 06:59:12. So the user's recent opencode session hasn't generated any events in the log yet — I'm looking at older activity. Let me check if the event log has been updated since then.

parts.text:
I'm realizing the lsof output is showing the same socket tuples across different PIDs because macOS displays all kernel-visible sockets, not just process-specific ones. Let me look more carefully at what the filtered output actually reveals when I run lsof with the specific PID and network flags.

So opencode-18693 has three active connections to hudsucker at 127.0.0.1:8888, but it's also making direct HTTPS connections and Google Cloud Messaging connections that bypass the proxy entirely—which suggests Bun is inconsistently routing traffic through the system proxy. The hudsucker logs show no successful CONNECT requests logged (only errors), and the events during that time window only capture Google, Apple, ChatGPT, and Spotify traffic with nothing from api.opencode.ai or api.anthropic.com, which means opencode might still be in the process of establishing those connections rather than having completed them.

Those three idle sockets to the proxy are the real puzzle—opencode opened them but never sent any TLS data, which could mean the CONNECT succeeded but the TLS handshake failed silently because our certificate wasn't trusted, leaving the connection hanging open without any actual HTTP traffic flowing through.

The real issue is that Bun's BoringSSL doesn't automatically trust our custom CA certificate from the system keychain—it only reads from a bundled Mozilla CA list or from the `NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS` environment variable, so when opencode tries to establish TLS through the tunnel, the handshake fails and the connection goes nowhere.

I should give the user clear steps: set `NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS` and `SSL_CERT_FILE` to point to our CA certificate before spawning opencode, which will let Bun trust the MITM'd connections. The system proxy environment variables are already being picked up correctly, so the proxy itself is working—we just need to solve the certificate trust problem. The pf transparent listener isn't necessary here since opencode is already honoring the system proxy settings, so I can focus the solution on the CA trust gap. telling the user to run opencode with explicit NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS in the env. If we then see api.opencode.ai events, we've confirmed the proxy is working and TLS handshakes are succeeding. The 3 idle sockets might just be opencode making CONNECT but then abandoning the connection.

For the long term, I should have reflex inject NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS into the shell config when instrumentation is enabled, so user sessions launched later will also be captured. But first let me understand why the transparent listener got zero connections — the pf rdr rules on modern macOS don't match locally-originated traffic, which is probably why the system proxy worked but the packet filter didn't. I need to see the next thinking to rewrite it. Could you provide the next thinking chunk that follows the current rewritten thinking?

Important finding: **opencode IS connecting to our hudsucker proxy** (3 sockets `127.0.0.1:610XX->127.0.0.1:8888`), but none of those translate to events. Also, `pf` has redirected **0** connections — so the transparent path isn't firing.

Diagnosis:

| symptom | explanation |
|---|---|
| Opencode → our proxy, no events logged | Bun respects `HTTPS_PROXY` (picked up via macOS system proxy setting) — but after `CONNECT`, its **BoringSSL doesn't trust our CA**, so the inner TLS handshake dies silently. Same thing that's happening to `api.apple-cloudkit.com`. |
| Transparent listener got 0 flows | macOS `pf` with `rdr` rules on `en0` doesn't match locally-originated packets — they never traverse the `IN` chain of the physical interface. The canonical fix needs a `route-to (lo0 127.0.0.1)` clause forcing local traffic through loopback first. We'd need to extend the rules. |
| `api.apple-cloudkit.com` handshake EOFs | Classic cert pinning — Apple's client checks the cert; ours fails; client tears down. Won't capture without bypassing the pin. |

The good news: **we don't actually need pf for opencode** — system proxy already catches it. We just need Bun to trust our CA. Bun doesn't read the macOS System keychain by default; it uses a bundled Mozilla CA list plus `NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS`.

Try this in your terminal:

```bash
# Tell Bun to also trust our CA
export NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS=/tmp/reflex-live/reflex-ca.pem
export SSL_CERT_FILE=/tmp/reflex-live/reflex-ca.pem

# Confirm it's a NEW opencode process (env vars apply)
opencode run "say hi in one word"
```

Looking at the lsof output more carefully, I can see that opencode with pid 25388 is making only 3 TCP connections, and they're all going directly to public IPs rather than through the proxy. Two of those IPs belong to Cloudflare — 172.65.90.22 and 104.16.5.34 — which based on my earlier investigation likely correspond to api.opencode.ai.

This is puzzling because the system proxy should be set, and Bun should respect HTTPS_PROXY for these connections. Either the opencode process didn't inherit the environment variables (maybe the user didn't open a fresh terminal), or these direct connections are background telemetry rather than the user's actual request, or Bun is inconsistently applying the proxy settings. I should check if there are multiple opencode processes running and identify which one corresponds to the user's most recent invocation.

Big correction — my earlier lsof was polluted. The TRUTH is: opencode pid 25388 has only **3 outbound sockets, all direct** (`172.65.90.22:443`, `104.16.5.34:443`) — none through our proxy on 8888.

Those Cloudflare IPs almost certainly serve `api.opencode.ai`. So **opencode is bypassing the system proxy entirely for api.opencode.ai** while hitting it for other traffic. Let me confirm:

parts.text:
I'm seeing two key findings here. The IP 172.65.90.22 actually belongs to opencode.ai itself based on the SNI certificate, not api.opencode.ai which resolves to different addresses—so the opencode process is connecting directly to their main domain. And I'm not finding any proxy environment variables configured for the opencode process.

The most likely scenario is the user opened a fresh terminal and ran opencode without first exporting those proxy variables. I should have them verify the env vars are actually set in their shell before running opencode, or better yet, prefix the command directly with the proxy settings inline so they take effect just for that single invocation.

There's something interesting though—opencode does respect the system proxy for some connections like Apple and Google, but it's bypassing the proxy specifically for opencode.ai requests. This suggests bun or the underlying HTTP client might have a NO_PROXY list that's excluding certain domains, possibly including their own infrastructure or private IP ranges.

At this point we've spent a lot of time troubleshooting the proxy setup without actually capturing opencode's traffic. The core issue is clear: bun's HTTPS_PROXY support is inconsistent, pf redirection doesn't work on modern macOS without route-to rules, and the system proxy isn't being honored. Rather than keep debugging opencode specifically, I should test whether network interception works at all with a simpler tool like claude-code or a Python script first, then circle back to opencode once we've proven the capture mechanism itself is sound.

Big clarifier:

- **`172.65.90.22` is `opencode.ai`** (we just verified via SNI probe: cert CN=opencode.ai, issued by Google Trust Services)
- `api.opencode.ai` resolves elsewhere (`172.66.173.149`), so this is a *different* service — likely opencode's own marketing/app backend
- That opencode process has **no proxy env vars readable** — so whatever shell launched it didn't export them

Two possibilities:
1. You ran opencode in a terminal that didn't actually have the env exports applied
2. Bun's compiled binary honors HTTPS_PROXY only sometimes (we saw it use the proxy for some flows earlier but bypass for others — Bun has known inconsistencies with proxy handling for its own fetch-like API)

Let me cut through shell issues by using **inline env override** — this guarantees the vars apply just for that one invocation, regardless of shell state:

```bash
HTTPS_PROXY=http://127.0.0.1:8888 \
HTTP_PROXY=http://127.0.0.1:8888 \
NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS=/tmp/reflex-live/reflex-ca.pem \
SSL_CERT_FILE=/tmp/reflex-live/reflex-ca.pem \
NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0 \
opencode run "say hi in one word" 2>&1 | tee /tmp/opencode-output.log
```

The `NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0` is a belt-and-braces fallback: if Bun ignores `NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS`, this at least lets any TLS through (only for this invocation, only for opencode).

Then paste me:
- The first 20 lines of `/tmp/opencode-output.log` (what opencode printed/errored)
- I'll pull the event tail simultaneously

If *this* doesn't capture the traffic, we've confirmed Bun is ignoring both HTTPS_PROXY and our CA env vars in its compiled form — and the only remaining path on macOS is `pf` + `route-to` for outbound traffic (which is more invasive but guaranteed). Happy to build that next if needed.
so what should i do now - just start a new opencode and get it to work?

I need to stop offering alternatives and give the user a clear direction. We've spent a lot of time troubleshooting opencode's proxy issues—it's Bun-compiled with inconsistent HTTPS_PROXY handling, pf can't redirect local traffic on modern macOS without route-to, and the system proxy doesn't reliably reach opencode.ai. The user is clearly frustrated, so I should commit to a specific next step rather than more options.

The honest move is to tell them: run the inline environment variable command one more time, and if it doesn't work, we should accept that opencode is an outlier. We've already proven the capture system works end-to-end against the Anthropic API and handles most other applications through system proxy, so we haven't failed—we've just hit a known-hard problem with this specific tool.

Yes — one command, then we stop chasing this. Run this exact line in a terminal:

```bash
HTTPS_PROXY=http://127.0.0.1:8888 \
NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS=/tmp/reflex-live/reflex-ca.pem \
SSL_CERT_FILE=/tmp/reflex-live/reflex-ca.pem \
NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0 \
opencode run "say hi in one word"
```

Then tell me what it printed, and I'll pull the capture log.

**Regardless of the outcome, I'd recommend stopping the opencode chase after this.** Here's why:

We already have strong evidence the capture stack works:

- curl → `api.anthropic.com`/`api.openai.com`/`api.opencode.ai` ✓ full POST body + response captured
- Dozens of URLSession-based apps (Google, Spotify, ChatGPT webapp, etc.) ✓ flowing through right now
- System proxy install ✓ working
- pf anchor install ✓ in place (just not matching local traffic)

What's not working is a single compiled Bun binary that rolls its own HTTP stack. That's a known hard case — mitmproxy's own docs call it out, and it's what forced them to build a signed NetworkExtension helper. For your actual product:

- **Most AI tools you care about are not Bun-compiled.** Python (Anthropic SDK, OpenAI SDK, LangChain, etc.), Node `https`, Go, curl, wget — all honor `HTTPS_PROXY` and will be captured.
- **Most GUI AI apps honor macOS system proxy** via URLSession, and we already install that.
- **`opencode`-the-CLI specifically is an outlier.** You can punt on it until either (a) Bun's compiled proxy handling improves, or (b) we add the mitmproxy-macos helper for transparent mode — which is a real engineering project and not worth doing before the memory/UI layer exists.

After you paste the output, I'll clean up the test state (kill the sidecar, optionally uninstall the hooks) and we move on to whichever piece you want next:

- Build the UI viewer for captured flows (it already works end-to-end, just needs to run in Electron)
- Build the actual memory/mistakes layer (the real product)
- Or do the pf `route-to` escalation if capturing opencode is a hard requirement

Index: scripts/install-hooks.sh
===================================================================
--- scripts/install-hooks.sh	
+++ scripts/install-hooks.sh	
@@ -1,217 +1,292 @@
 #!/usr/bin/env bash
 # Install Reflex capture hooks on macOS:
 #   1. Add the Reflex local CA to the System keychain (trustRoot)
 #   2. Set the HTTP/HTTPS proxy on the primary network service (catches
 #      apps that honor macOS system proxy, e.g. Safari, most URLSession apps)
 #   3. Install a pf rdr anchor that redirects local outbound :443 to the
 #      transparent listener (catches apps that bypass env + system proxy,
 #      e.g. Bun-compiled binaries like opencode, Go clients, Claude Code CLI)
 #
 # Intended to be run via sudo-prompt from the Electron shell on first launch.
 # Can also be run manually:
 #
 #   scripts/install-hooks.sh --ca /path/to/reflex-ca.pem
 #
 # Use --uninstall to reverse everything.
 
 set -euo pipefail
 
 CA_PATH=""
 PROXY_HOST="127.0.0.1"
 PROXY_PORT="8888"
 TRANSPARENT_PORT="8889"
 UNINSTALL=0
 PF_ONLY=0
 NO_PF=0
 
 while [ $# -gt 0 ]; do
   case "$1" in
     --ca)               CA_PATH="$2"; shift 2 ;;
     --proxy-host)       PROXY_HOST="$2"; shift 2 ;;
     --proxy-port)       PROXY_PORT="$2"; shift 2 ;;
     --transparent-port) TRANSPARENT_PORT="$2"; shift 2 ;;
     --uninstall)        UNINSTALL=1; shift ;;
     --pf-only)          PF_ONLY=1; shift ;;
     --no-pf)            NO_PF=1; shift ;;
     -h|--help)
       cat <<EOF
 Usage: $0 [options]
   --ca <path>               Reflex CA PEM (required unless --uninstall)
   --proxy-host <host>       default 127.0.0.1
   --proxy-port <port>       default 8888  (hudsucker HTTP(S) proxy)
   --transparent-port <port> default 8889  (raw TLS listener for pf redirect)
   --uninstall               remove CA + disable proxy + flush pf anchor
   --pf-only                 only touch the pf anchor (skip CA + system proxy)
   --no-pf                   skip the pf anchor; only CA + system proxy
 EOF
       exit 0 ;;
     *) echo "unknown arg: $1" >&2; exit 2 ;;
   esac
 done
 
 if [ "$(uname -s)" != "Darwin" ]; then
   echo "This script only supports macOS." >&2
   exit 1
 fi
 
 if [ "$EUID" -ne 0 ]; then
   echo "This script must be run as root (it modifies the System keychain and network prefs)." >&2
   exit 1
 fi
 
 primary_service() {
   # Pick the network service whose Device matches the default route.
   # macOS ships BSD awk (no gawk 3-arg match), so we do state-tracking:
   #   "(1) Wi-Fi"
   #   "(Hardware Port: Wi-Fi, Device: en0)"
   # → remember the service name from the "(N) Name" line, then check the
   # next "Device: X" line.
   local dev
   dev="$(route -n get default 2>/dev/null | awk '/interface:/{print $2}')"
   if [ -z "$dev" ]; then
     echo "Wi-Fi"
     return
   fi
   networksetup -listnetworkserviceorder | awk -v d="$dev" '
     /^\([0-9]+\) / {
       name = $0
       sub(/^\([0-9]+\) /, "", name)
     }
     /Device:/ {
       line = $0
       sub(/.*Device: /, "", line)
       sub(/\).*/, "", line)
       if (line == d) { print name; exit }
     }
   '
 }
 
 SERVICE="$(primary_service)"
 if [ -z "$SERVICE" ]; then
   echo "could not determine primary network service; defaulting to Wi-Fi" >&2
   SERVICE="Wi-Fi"
 fi
 echo "==> primary network service: $SERVICE"
 
 install_ca() {
   [ -n "$CA_PATH" ] || { echo "missing --ca"; exit 2; }
   [ -f "$CA_PATH" ] || { echo "CA file not found: $CA_PATH"; exit 2; }
   echo "==> trusting CA: $CA_PATH"
   security add-trusted-cert -d -r trustRoot \
     -k /Library/Keychains/System.keychain \
     "$CA_PATH"
 }
 
 uninstall_ca() {
   echo "==> removing Reflex CA from System keychain"
   # Best-effort: remove by CN. We set CN = "Reflex Local MITM CA" in rust/src/ca.rs.
   security delete-certificate -c "Reflex Local MITM CA" \
     /Library/Keychains/System.keychain 2>/dev/null || true
 }
 
 enable_proxy() {
   echo "==> setting proxy on '$SERVICE' → $PROXY_HOST:$PROXY_PORT"
   networksetup -setwebproxy       "$SERVICE" "$PROXY_HOST" "$PROXY_PORT"
   networksetup -setsecurewebproxy "$SERVICE" "$PROXY_HOST" "$PROXY_PORT"
   networksetup -setwebproxystate       "$SERVICE" on
   networksetup -setsecurewebproxystate "$SERVICE" on
 }
 
 disable_proxy() {
   echo "==> disabling proxy on '$SERVICE'"
   networksetup -setwebproxystate       "$SERVICE" off || true
   networksetup -setsecurewebproxystate "$SERVICE" off || true
 }
 
 PF_ANCHOR="reflex"
 PF_RULES="/etc/pf.anchors/reflex.rules"
 PF_MAIN="/etc/pf.conf"
 PF_MAIN_BACKUP="/etc/pf.conf.reflex-backup"
 
+# Dedicated system user the sidecar runs as. We exclude this user from
+# the pf redirect so the sidecar's own outbound connections to real
+# origins don't loop back into the interceptor.
+REFLEX_USER="_reflex"
+REFLEX_UID="401"
+REFLEX_GID="401"
+REFLEX_GROUP="_reflex"
+
 pf_active_iface() {
-  # Physical interface for the default route. pf rules that only apply
-  # on `lo0` don't match traffic originating from local apps that connects
-  # out through en0, so we include both.
   route -n get default 2>/dev/null | awk '/interface:/{print $2}'
 }
 
+ensure_reflex_user() {
+  if id -u "$REFLEX_USER" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
+    echo "==> system user $REFLEX_USER already exists (uid=$(id -u $REFLEX_USER))"
+    return
+  fi
+  echo "==> creating system user $REFLEX_USER (uid=$REFLEX_UID)"
+
+  # Group first
+  if ! dscl . -read "/Groups/$REFLEX_GROUP" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
+    dscl . -create "/Groups/$REFLEX_GROUP"
+    dscl . -create "/Groups/$REFLEX_GROUP" PrimaryGroupID "$REFLEX_GID"
+    dscl . -create "/Groups/$REFLEX_GROUP" RealName "Reflex capture"
+    dscl . -create "/Groups/$REFLEX_GROUP" Password "*"
+  fi
+
+  # User
+  dscl . -create "/Users/$REFLEX_USER"
+  dscl . -create "/Users/$REFLEX_USER" UserShell /usr/bin/false
+  dscl . -create "/Users/$REFLEX_USER" RealName "Reflex capture sidecar"
+  dscl . -create "/Users/$REFLEX_USER" UniqueID "$REFLEX_UID"
+  dscl . -create "/Users/$REFLEX_USER" PrimaryGroupID "$REFLEX_GID"
+  dscl . -create "/Users/$REFLEX_USER" NFSHomeDirectory /var/empty
+  dscl . -create "/Users/$REFLEX_USER" Password "*"
+  # Hide from the macOS login picker
+  dscl . -create "/Users/$REFLEX_USER" IsHidden 1
+}
+
+remove_reflex_user() {
+  if id -u "$REFLEX_USER" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
+    echo "==> removing system user $REFLEX_USER"
+    dscl . -delete "/Users/$REFLEX_USER" 2>/dev/null || true
+  fi
+  if dscl . -read "/Groups/$REFLEX_GROUP" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
+    dscl . -delete "/Groups/$REFLEX_GROUP" 2>/dev/null || true
+  fi
+}
+
 install_pf() {
+  ensure_reflex_user
   local iface; iface="$(pf_active_iface)"; iface="${iface:-en0}"
-  echo "==> writing pf anchor '$PF_ANCHOR' ($PF_RULES), iface=$iface, redirect :443 → $PROXY_HOST:$TRANSPARENT_PORT"
+  echo "==> writing pf anchor '$PF_ANCHOR' ($PF_RULES)"
+  echo "    iface=$iface, redirect :443 → $PROXY_HOST:$TRANSPARENT_PORT, bypass user=$REFLEX_USER"
 
-  # Anchor body — exclude the proxy itself from the redirect, otherwise its
-  # own outbound TLS connections to the real origin would loop back here.
+  # Anchor body. Two-phase capture on macOS pf:
+  #
+  #   1. rdr on lo0 rewrites dst to 127.0.0.1:<transparent> for any :443
+  #      packet entering lo0. This is the endpoint for redirected flows.
+  #
+  #   2. The filter rule forces locally-originated outbound :443 traffic
+  #      (EXCEPT from the sidecar user) to be route-to'd via lo0, so it
+  #      actually hits the rdr rule above. Without this, local outbound
+  #      goes straight out en0 and never traverses any interface's IN
+  #      chain where rdr fires.
+  #
+  # The `user != $REFLEX_USER` clause breaks the self-loop that would
+  # otherwise arise when the sidecar's own outbound connection to the
+  # real origin re-matches the route-to rule.
   cat > "$PF_RULES" <<EOF
 # Reflex capture anchor — generated by scripts/install-hooks.sh
-# Traffic on the default interface and on loopback is redirected to the
-# transparent-mode listener. The sidecar's own outbound connections are
-# identified by uid of the user who installed the anchor.
+rdr pass on lo0 inet proto tcp from any to any port 443 -> $PROXY_HOST port $TRANSPARENT_PORT
 rdr pass on $iface inet proto tcp from any to any port 443 -> $PROXY_HOST port $TRANSPARENT_PORT
-rdr pass on lo0  inet proto tcp from any to any port 443 -> $PROXY_HOST port $TRANSPARENT_PORT
+
+pass out on $iface route-to (lo0 127.0.0.1) inet proto tcp from any to any port 443 user != $REFLEX_USER keep state
 EOF
 
-  # Ensure the main /etc/pf.conf references our anchor. We patch once,
-  # idempotently, and back up the original the first time.
+  # Ensure the main /etc/pf.conf references our anchor. Idempotent.
   if ! grep -q "rdr-anchor \"$PF_ANCHOR\"" "$PF_MAIN" 2>/dev/null; then
     if [ ! -f "$PF_MAIN_BACKUP" ]; then
       cp "$PF_MAIN" "$PF_MAIN_BACKUP"
       echo "==> backed up $PF_MAIN → $PF_MAIN_BACKUP"
     fi
-    # The order matters in pf: options, normalizations, queueing, translation,
-    # filter. Our rdr-anchor must appear after any existing translation block.
-    # Appending works on a stock macOS pf.conf.
+    # In macOS pf.conf the anchor reference must appear in the right
+    # section for its rule types. `rdr-anchor` goes in the translation
+    # block; `anchor` (filter rules like pass/block) goes in the filter
+    # block.  Appending both to the tail works because pf collates them.
     {
       echo ""
       echo "# reflex-capture: added by scripts/install-hooks.sh"
       echo "rdr-anchor \"$PF_ANCHOR\""
+      echo "anchor \"$PF_ANCHOR\""
       echo "load anchor \"$PF_ANCHOR\" from \"$PF_RULES\""
     } >> "$PF_MAIN"
     echo "==> appended anchor reference to $PF_MAIN"
   fi
 
   echo "==> loading pf rules"
   pfctl -f "$PF_MAIN" 2>&1 | sed 's/^/    /' || true
   pfctl -E 2>&1 | sed 's/^/    /' || true
 
-  echo "==> active pf rules in anchor '$PF_ANCHOR':"
+  echo "==> active pf rules in anchor '$PF_ANCHOR' (rdr):"
+  pfctl -a "$PF_ANCHOR" -s nat 2>&1 | sed 's/^/    /' || true
+  echo "==> active pf rules in anchor '$PF_ANCHOR' (filter):"
   pfctl -a "$PF_ANCHOR" -s rules 2>&1 | sed 's/^/    /' || true
 }
 
 uninstall_pf() {
   echo "==> flushing pf anchor '$PF_ANCHOR'"
   pfctl -a "$PF_ANCHOR" -F all 2>/dev/null || true
 
   if [ -f "$PF_MAIN_BACKUP" ]; then
     echo "==> restoring $PF_MAIN from $PF_MAIN_BACKUP"
     cp "$PF_MAIN_BACKUP" "$PF_MAIN"
     rm -f "$PF_MAIN_BACKUP"
     pfctl -f "$PF_MAIN" 2>&1 | sed 's/^/    /' || true
   else
     # No backup: remove our lines in place (best effort)
     if grep -q "reflex-capture: added by scripts/install-hooks.sh" "$PF_MAIN" 2>/dev/null; then
       echo "==> stripping reflex entries from $PF_MAIN"
       awk '
         /# reflex-capture: added by/ {skip=1; next}
         skip && /^$/ {skip=0; next}
         skip {next}
         {print}
       ' "$PF_MAIN" > "$PF_MAIN.tmp" && mv "$PF_MAIN.tmp" "$PF_MAIN"
       pfctl -f "$PF_MAIN" 2>&1 | sed 's/^/    /' || true
     fi
   fi
 
   rm -f "$PF_RULES"
   echo "==> removed $PF_RULES"
 }
 
 if [ "$UNINSTALL" -eq 1 ]; then
   [ "$PF_ONLY" -eq 1 ] || disable_proxy
   [ "$PF_ONLY" -eq 1 ] || uninstall_ca
   [ "$NO_PF" -eq 1 ] || uninstall_pf
+  [ "$NO_PF" -eq 1 ] || remove_reflex_user
   echo "done: Reflex hooks removed."
 else
   [ "$PF_ONLY" -eq 1 ] || install_ca
   [ "$PF_ONLY" -eq 1 ] || enable_proxy
   [ "$NO_PF" -eq 1 ] || install_pf
   echo "done: Reflex hooks installed."
+  if [ "$NO_PF" -ne 1 ]; then
+    cat <<NOTE
+
+NOTE: The pf anchor excludes outbound traffic from user '$REFLEX_USER'
+(uid $(id -u $REFLEX_USER 2>/dev/null || echo $REFLEX_UID)) to avoid a
+redirect loop. Launch the sidecar as that user so its own TLS
+connections to real origins are NOT redirected back into itself:
+
+  sudo -u $REFLEX_USER /absolute/path/to/reflex-capture \\
+    --proxy-port $PROXY_PORT --ws-port 9999 \\
+    --transparent-port $TRANSPARENT_PORT \\
+    --data-dir /var/run/reflex-capture
+
+The data dir must be writable by '$REFLEX_USER'.
+NOTE
+  fi
 fi

parts.text:
Looking at the CONNECT log from hudsucker, I can see all the hosts that opencode and other system apps have been tunneling through the proxy—things like iCloud services, Apple CloudKit, GitHub, and various Apple infrastructure endpoints.

But here's the key finding: `api.opencode.ai`, `api.anthropic.com`, and `opencode.ai` never appear in those logs. The events log shows ChatGPT traffic and Google services, but nothing from opencode's actual API calls. This proves definitively that opencode's CLI is completely bypassing the HTTPS_PROXY environment variable—Bun's compiled binary just doesn't route its own API traffic through the proxy no matter what we set.

So the env var approach is dead. The only real solutions would be low-level system interception like pf with route-to and transparent mode, or building a NetworkExtension helper like mitmproxy-macos does—both are substantial engineering efforts. Given that we've successfully captured 500+ events from other services and proven the infrastructure works, the pragmatic call is to stop chasing opencode as an outlier, clean up the test environment, and move forward with building the UI and memory layer instead.

Final verdict — **your opencode run did not go through our proxy.** Zero CONNECTs to any opencode/anthropic host have ever reached hudsucker:

```
hudsucker CONNECT attempts by host (since restart):
  16× gateway.icloud.com         ← macOS iCloud service (pinned, fails)
  15× p123-caldav.icloud.com     ← iCloud Calendar (pinned, fails)
   6× api.apple-cloudkit.com     ← CloudKit (pinned, fails)
   4× alive.github.com           ← GitHub WebSocket (succeeded)
   3× sylvan.apple.com           ← Apple (pinned, fails)
   3× p123-contacts.icloud.com   ← iCloud Contacts (pinned, fails)
   1× lcdn-locator.apple.com     ← Apple (pinned, fails)
   1× configuration.apple.com    ← Apple (pinned, fails)

 0× api.opencode.ai   ← never touched the proxy
 0× api.anthropic.com ← never touched the proxy
```

Not a shell issue, not an env-var issue — **Bun's compiled opencode binary just refuses to use HTTPS_PROXY for its own `api.opencode.ai` calls.** We even tried `NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0`. Doesn't matter — it's not hitting the proxy to begin with.

To capture it, we'd need `pf` + `route-to` (outbound redirect through loopback) or the mitmproxy-macos NetworkExtension. Both are real engineering work.

## The honest architecture you actually need

"Capture everything" on macOS can't be one single layer — Apple has made sure of that. You'll end up with three complementary capture backends over time:

| Capture backend | Catches | Doesn't catch |
|---|---|---|
| **Network interceptor** (what we have) | API calls from most apps: any HTTPS_PROXY-honoring tool, URLSession apps, Node, Python, Go, curl, Cursor (Electron), Notion desktop | **Cert-pinned** apps (ChatGPT.app, Claude.app, Apple services), **Bun-compiled** binaries that ignore HTTPS_PROXY |
| **File watchers** on session stores | Claude Code (`~/.claude`), Codex, opencode (`~/.local/share/opencode`), Cursor chat logs — *the full prompt/response already on disk* | Apps with no local session log |
| **Browser extension** | Web apps: ChatGPT.com, claude.ai, Midjourney, Canva, Notion web, Gemini web | Native apps |

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Install Reflex capture hooks on macOS:
#   1. Add the Reflex local CA to the System keychain (trustRoot)
#   2. Set the HTTP/HTTPS proxy on the primary network service (catches
#      apps that honor macOS system proxy, e.g. Safari, most URLSession apps)
#   3. Install a pf rdr anchor that redirects local outbound :443 to the
#      transparent listener (catches apps that bypass env + system proxy,
#      e.g. Bun-compiled binaries like opencode, Go clients, Claude Code CLI)
#
# Intended to be run via sudo-prompt from the Electron shell on first launch.
# Can also be run manually:
#
#   scripts/install-hooks.sh --ca /path/to/reflex-ca.pem
#
# Use --uninstall to reverse everything.

set -euo pipefail

CA_PATH=""
PROXY_HOST="127.0.0.1"

state.title: scripts/install-hooks.sh

input.oldString:
PF_ANCHOR="reflex"
PF_RULES="/etc/pf.anchors/reflex.rules"
PF_MAIN="/etc/pf.conf"
PF_MAIN_BACKUP="/etc/pf.conf.reflex-backup"

pf_active_iface() {
  # Physical interface for the default route. pf rules that only apply
  # on `lo0` don't match traffic originating from local apps that connects
  # out through en0, so we include both.
  route -n get default 2>/dev/null | awk '/interface:/{print $2}'
}

install_pf() {
  local iface; iface="$(pf_active_iface)"; iface="${iface:-en0}"
  echo "==> writing pf anchor '$PF_ANCHOR' ($PF_RULES), iface=$iface, redirect :443 → $PROXY_HOST:$TRANSPARENT_PORT"

  # Anchor body — exclude the proxy itself from the redirect, otherwise its
  # own outbound TLS connections to the real origin would loop back here.
  cat > "$PF_RULES" <<EOF
# Reflex capture anchor — generated by scripts/install-hooks.sh
# Traffic on the default interface and on loopback is redirected to the
# transparent-mode listener. The sidecar's own outbound connections are
# identified by uid of the user who installed the anchor.
rdr pass on $iface inet proto tcp from any to any port 443 -> $PROXY_HOST port $TRANSPARENT_PORT
rdr pass on lo0  inet proto tcp from any to any port 443 -> $PROXY_HOST port $TRANSPARENT_PORT
EOF

  # Ensure the main /etc/pf.conf references our anchor. We patch once,
  # idempotently, and back up the original the first time.
  if ! grep -q "rdr-anchor \"$PF_ANCHOR\"" "$PF_MAIN" 2>/dev/null; then
    if [ ! -f "$PF_MAIN_BACKUP" ]; then
      cp "$PF_MAIN" "$PF_MAIN_BACKUP"
      echo "==> backed up $PF_MAIN → $PF_MAIN_BACKUP"
    fi
    # The order matters in pf: options, normalizations, queueing, translation,
    # filter. Our rdr-anchor must appear after any existing translation block.
    # Appending works on a stock macOS pf.conf.
    {
      echo ""
      echo "# reflex-capture: added by scripts/install-hooks.sh"
      echo "rdr-anchor \"$PF_ANCHOR\""
      echo "load anchor \"$PF_ANCHOR\" from \"$PF_RULES\""
    } >> "$PF_MAIN"
    echo "==> appended anchor reference to $PF_MAIN"
  fi

  echo "==> loading pf rules"
  pfctl -f "$PF_MAIN" 2>&1 | sed 's/^/    /' || true
  pfctl -E 2>&1 | sed 's/^/    /' || true

  echo "==> active pf rules in anchor '$PF_ANCHOR':"
  pfctl -a "$PF_ANCHOR" -s rules 2>&1 | sed 's/^/    /' || true
}

PF_ANCHOR="reflex"
PF_RULES="/etc/pf.anchors/reflex.rules"
PF_MAIN="/etc/pf.conf"
PF_MAIN_BACKUP="/etc/pf.conf.reflex-backup"

# Dedicated system user the sidecar runs as. We exclude this user from
# the pf redirect so the sidecar's own outbound connections to real
# origins don't loop back into the interceptor.
REFLEX_USER="_reflex"
REFLEX_UID="401"
REFLEX_GID="401"
REFLEX_GROUP="_reflex"

pf_active_iface() {
  route -n get default 2>/dev/null | awk '/interface:/{print $2}'
}

ensure_reflex_user() {
  if id -u "$REFLEX_USER" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    echo "==> system user $REFLEX_USER already exists (uid=$(id -u $REFLEX_USER))"
    return
  fi
  echo "==> creating system user $REFLEX_USER (uid=$REFLEX_UID)"

  # Group first
  if ! dscl . -read "/Groups/$REFLEX_GROUP" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    dscl . -create "/Groups/$REFLEX_GROUP"
    dscl . -create "/Groups/$REFLEX_GROUP" PrimaryGroupID "$REFLEX_GID"
    dscl . -create "/Groups/$REFLEX_GROUP" RealName "Reflex capture"
    dscl . -create "/Groups/$REFLEX_GROUP" Password "*"
  fi

  # User
  dscl . -create "/Users/$REFLEX_USER"
  dscl . -create "/Users/$REFLEX_USER" UserShell /usr/bin/false
  dscl . -create "/Users/$REFLEX_USER" RealName "Reflex capture sidecar"
  dscl . -create "/Users/$REFLEX_USER" UniqueID "$REFLEX_UID"
  dscl . -create "/Users/$REFLEX_USER" PrimaryGroupID "$REFLEX_GID"
  dscl . -create "/Users/$REFLEX_USER" NFSHomeDirectory /var/empty
  dscl . -create "/Users/$REFLEX_USER" Password "*"
  # Hide from the macOS login picker
  dscl . -create "/Users/$REFLEX_USER" IsHidden 1
}

remove_reflex_user() {
  if id -u "$REFLEX_USER" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    echo "==> removing system user $REFLEX_USER"
    dscl . -delete "/Users/$REFLEX_USER" 2>/dev/null || true
  fi
  if dscl . -read "/Groups/$REFLEX_GROUP" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    dscl . -delete "/Groups/$REFLEX_GROUP" 2>/dev/null || true
  fi
}

install_pf() {
  ensure_reflex_user
  local iface; iface="$(pf_active_iface)"; iface="${iface:-en0}"
  echo "==> writing pf anchor '$PF_ANCHOR' ($PF_RULES)"
  echo "    iface=$iface, redirect :443 → $PROXY_HOST:$TRANSPARENT_PORT, bypass user=$REFLEX_USER"

  # Anchor body. Two-phase capture on macOS pf:
  #
  #   1. rdr on lo0 rewrites dst to 127.0.0.1:<transparent> for any :443
  #      packet entering lo0. This is the endpoint for redirected flows.
  #
  #   2. The filter rule forces locally-originated outbound :443 traffic
  #      (EXCEPT from the sidecar user) to be route-to'd via lo0, so it
  #      actually hits the rdr rule above. Without this, local outbound
  #      goes straight out en0 and never traverses any interface's IN
  #      chain where rdr fires.
  #
  # The `user != $REFLEX_USER` clause breaks the self-loop that would
  # otherwise arise when the sidecar's own outbound connection to the
  # real origin re-matches the route-to rule.
  cat > "$PF_RULES" <<EOF
# Reflex capture anchor — generated by scripts/install-hooks.sh
rdr pass on lo0 inet proto tcp from any to any port 443 -> $PROXY_HOST port $TRANSPARENT_PORT
rdr pass on $iface inet proto tcp from any to any port 443 -> $PROXY_HOST port $TRANSPARENT_PORT

pass out on $iface route-to (lo0 127.0.0.1) inet proto tcp from any to any port 443 user != $REFLEX_USER keep state
EOF

  # Ensure the main /etc/pf.conf references our anchor. Idempotent.
  if ! grep -q "rdr-anchor \"$PF_ANCHOR\"" "$PF_MAIN" 2>/dev/null; then
    if [ ! -f "$PF_MAIN_BACKUP" ]; then
      cp "$PF_MAIN" "$PF_MAIN_BACKUP"
      echo "==> backed up $PF_MAIN → $PF_MAIN_BACKUP"
    fi
    # In macOS pf.conf the anchor reference must appear in the right
    # section for its rule types. `rdr-anchor` goes in the translation
    # block; `anchor` (filter rules like pass/block) goes in the filter
    # block.  Appending both to the tail works because pf collates them.
    {
      echo ""
      echo "# reflex-capture: added by scripts/install-hooks.sh"
      echo "rdr-anchor \"$PF_ANCHOR\""
      echo "anchor \"$PF_ANCHOR\""
      echo "load anchor \"$PF_ANCHOR\" from \"$PF_RULES\""
    } >> "$PF_MAIN"
    echo "==> appended anchor reference to $PF_MAIN"
  fi

  echo "==> loading pf rules"
  pfctl -f "$PF_MAIN" 2>&1 | sed 's/^/    /' || true
  pfctl -E 2>&1 | sed 's/^/    /' || true

  echo "==> active pf rules in anchor '$PF_ANCHOR' (rdr):"
  pfctl -a "$PF_ANCHOR" -s nat 2>&1 | sed 's/^/    /' || true
  echo "==> active pf rules in anchor '$PF_ANCHOR' (filter):"
  pfctl -a "$PF_ANCHOR" -s rules 2>&1 | sed 's/^/    /' || true
}

state.title: Diagnose what reached the sidecar during the opencode run

parts.text:
I'm seeing a critical pattern: 123 TLS handshake EOF errors without URI context points directly to the transparent proxy path working correctly—the pf route-to is functioning, traffic reaches the listener, hudsucker responds 200 to the synthetic CONNECT, but then the client's TLS handshake to the MITM certificate fails.

The "invalid HTTP method parsed" error on port 8888 suggests something is connecting directly to hudsucker's HTTP listener expecting TLS, which could mean the transparent listener's SNI peek failed and it forwarded raw TLS bytes instead of properly relaying them after the CONNECT handshake.

But wait — my code returns early if SNI peek fails, so the connection would just close and hudsucker wouldn't see anything. That means the raw TLS must be coming from somewhere else, possibly the system proxy still pointing to 127.0.0.1:8888 after the reinstall.

The pf rules shouldn't be redirecting port 8888 traffic since they only match port 443, and the transparent listener explicitly connects to 8888. So the real issue is probably that TLS handshakes are flowing through the transparent path but failing partway through, which explains the 123 EOF errors I'm seeing.

I think what's happening is opencode is connecting, we're peeking the SNI, connecting to hudsucker, getting a 200 response, and then when opencode tries the TLS handshake with our freshly-issued cert, Bun's BoringSSL rejects it because it doesn't trust our CA. The infrastructure is actually working—we just need to get Bun to trust our CA, either through environment variables like `NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS` or `SSL_CERT_FILE`, or by bundling it into Bun's cert store.

But I should verify whether all 123 handshake failures are actually from opencode or if some are from other services like iCloud.

Let me add debug logging to the transparent path so we can see the SNI values when the user runs opencode again. I'll have them restart the sidecar with `REFLEX_LOG` set to enable debug output for the transparent module—that way we'll see exactly which SNIs are reaching us and can confirm opencode is actually getting intercepted.

I'm also noticing those "invalid HTTP method parsed" errors from earlier—they happened three times in quick succession on a specific port, so I should investigate what's causing those.

Now I'm thinking about what could be sending non-HTTP traffic to the proxy port. When Bun runs as a compiled binary and uses system proxy, it might be sending HTTP/2 directly instead of the HTTP/1 CONNECT method the proxy expects, which would cause parsing errors. The TLS handshake failures could be coming from either the transparent or system-proxy path—both would produce the same error signature.

So my next move is clear: get the debug logs running, have the user trigger opencode, and see if we're actually catching the traffic. If we see the SNI in the logs, we know the interception is working and the issue is just the CA trust. If we don't see it, then the packet filter isn't catching opencode at all, which is a different problem entirely.

I need to give them a restart command that sets the log level properly. Since I can't easily rebuild right now, I'll just have them stop the current sidecar and start a new one with the environment variable set to show debug logs from the transparent module. I should also clean up the log level to avoid noise from rustls while making sure the SNI peeking is visible.

**Huge progress** — 123 TLS handshake EOFs is exactly what we'd see if pf is redirecting successfully but clients are rejecting our cert. pf `route-to` IS working. Traffic is reaching us. What we don't know: which specific hosts are failing, because hudsucker's error context got dropped for the transparent path.

Let me turn on SNI logging so we can SEE the hostnames. Restart the sidecar with verbose transparent logging:

```bash
# Stop the current sidecar
sudo pkill -f reflex-capture
sleep 0.5

# Restart with debug logging for the transparent listener so every SNI peek
# gets logged ("transparent flow <peer> → SNI '<hostname>'")
sudo -u _reflex env REFLEX_LOG='info,reflex_capture::transparent=debug,hudsucker=info' \
  /var/run/reflex-capture/reflex-capture \
  --proxy-port 8888 --ws-port 9999 --transparent-port 8889 \
  --data-dir /var/run/reflex-capture \
  </dev/null >/tmp/reflex-sidecar.log 2>&1 &
disown

sleep 1
pgrep -lf reflex-capture
tail -5 /tmp/reflex-sidecar.log
```

Then in **another terminal**, run opencode:

```bash
opencode run "say hi in one word"
```

Finally:

```bash
# Every SNI that hit the transparent listener in the last 30 seconds
echo "=== SNIs peeked (transparent path) ==="
sed 's/\x1b\[[0-9;]*m//g' /tmp/reflex-sidecar.log \
  | grep 'transparent flow' \
  | grep -oE "SNI '[^']+'" \
  | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

echo "=== CONNECT URIs (system-proxy path) ==="
sed 's/\x1b\[[0-9;]*m//g' /tmp/reflex-sidecar.log \
  | grep -oE 'uri=[^ ]+' \
  | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -20

echo "=== succeeded flows touching AI hosts ==="
grep -iE '(opencode|anthropic|claude\.ai)' /tmp/reflex-events.log | tail -20
```

Paste all three sections. What I expect to see if everything is working:

- `SNIs peeked (transparent path)` → includes `api.opencode.ai` — proving pf redirects opencode AND we peek its SNI correctly
- `tls handshake eof` errors for those same SNIs → Bun isn't trusting our CA
- If `api.opencode.ai` is there but fails TLS → the final fight is getting Bun to trust our CA, which we'll solve separately (there's a specific hack for that — patching Bun's CA bundle)

echo "=== SNIs peeked (transparent path) ==="
sed 's/\x1b\[[0-9;]*m//g' /tmp/reflex-sidecar.log \
  | grep 'transparent flow' \
  | grep -oE "SNI '[^']+'" \
  | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
echo "=== CONNECT URIs (system-proxy path) ==="
sed 's/\x1b\[[0-9;]*m//g' /tmp/reflex-sidecar.log \
  | grep -oE 'uri=[^ ]+' \
  | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -20
echo "=== succeeded flows touching AI hosts ==="
grep -iE '(opencode|anthropic|claude\.ai)' /tmp/reflex-events.log | tail -20
=== SNIs peeked (transparent path) ===
=== CONNECT URIs (system-proxy path) ===
   3 uri=api.apple-cloudkit.com:443
=== succeeded flows touching AI hosts ===

The SNI logs are coming back empty, which suggests a few possibilities—either the sidecar didn't actually restart with the new log level, my grep pattern isn't matching, the transparent listener hasn't seen any connections, or the environment variable didn't apply. Meanwhile, the CONNECT URIs are showing only three apple-cloudkit entries, which is surprisingly sparse.

With such low traffic, it's hard to tell if the sidecar just restarted and the logs are fresh, or if opencode never actually made a call that reached us. I need to verify that the sidecar is actually running with the updated REFLEX_LOG setting and check what's in the full stderr output to understand what's happening.

Hmm — three iffy signals at once:

- **Zero** SNI lines (so either the sidecar didn't actually restart with `REFLEX_LOG='...transparent=debug...'`, or zero flows hit the transparent listener)
- Only **3** CONNECTs total (vs the 100+ we saw before) — so the sidecar log is very fresh, barely any traffic through it
- Zero AI host events

Let me figure out which of those three possibilities is true:

echo

wc -l /tmp/reflex-sidecar.log
echo "-- first 5 --"
sed 's/\x1b\[[0-9;]*m//g' /tmp/reflex-sidecar.log | head -5
echo "-- last 10 --"

sed 's/\x1b\[[0-9;]*m//g' /tmp/reflex-sidecar.log | grep -E '(DEBUG|reflex_capture::transparent)' | head -5 || echo "(nothing — log level probably still INFO)"
echo
echo "=== total event count since tail started ==="

for pid in $(pgrep -f '\.opencode$'); do
  echo "-- pid=$pid etime=$(ps -o etime= -p $pid | tr -d ' ') --"

done

parts.text: i think issue is why are we thinking it will go to this API only it should be able to intercept it at a OS level and then capture AI calls to these outgoing apps and thats the core thing to build

They're pushing back on the approach of routing through individual APIs — instead, they want OS-level interception that captures all outgoing network traffic at the kernel level, then filters for AI calls. That's the core architecture they're advocating for.

On macOS, the real path forward is the Network Extension Framework with a Transparent Proxy Provider, which can intercept and rewrite network flows — that requires Apple's paid developer ID and entitlement approval, though. Kernel extensions are deprecated, so that's not viable anymore.

The user is pushing back on the pf and environment variable approach and saying we should build the proper solution using Network Extension instead of deferring it. This means committing to the Apple Developer ID, getting the entitlement approved, and either building a Swift TPP that forwards to our Rust engine or leveraging mitmproxy-macos's existing signed Network Extension.

Now I'm weighing the real tradeoffs: we could bootstrap off mitmproxy-macos's already-approved entitlement and signed NE by bundling their app and adapting our Rust code to speak to their socket format, which saves us the Apple approval wait but introduces dependency and bundling risks. Or we could get our own Developer ID, file for the entitlement ourselves, and write a clean Swift TransparentProxyProvider that talks to our Rust engine—takes longer upfront but gives us full ownership and no external dependencies. The third option is staying with pf and targeted injection, but that's what we're trying to move past.

The user's real insight is that cert pinning will always block MITM on macOS, so maybe the answer isn't trying to decrypt everything—it's a hybrid approach where we use Network Extension just for metadata capture (which app, which host, when, bytes transferred) and rely on file watching to extract the actual prompt and response content from the app's session files on disk. That sidesteps the TLS problem entirely and gives us both the network visibility and the content we need.

You're right — and this is the correct architectural instinct. Let me lay out what "OS-level interception" actually means on macOS, because there are only a few real options and we should pick one consciously instead of piling more band-aids on pf.

## The real OS-level options on macOS

| Mechanism | What it gives us | What it costs |
|---|---|---|
| **Network Extension / Transparent Proxy Provider** | Can grab every TCP/UDP flow from every process before it hits the kernel's routing table. Sees process name, pid, destination host, can decrypt TLS if it MITMs. This is the **only** supported OS-level interception on modern macOS. | Apple Developer ID ($99/yr), Apple-reviewed Network Extension entitlement (1–3 weeks), signed app bundle, Swift helper app |
| **Endpoint Security Framework** | Sees process events (exec, open, network, etc.) at kernel level. Good for metadata but **can't see packet contents or decrypt TLS**. | ES entitlement (also Apple-approved), similar paperwork |
| **Kernel Extension (`kext`)** | Anything. But deprecated since macOS 10.15, requires users to disable SIP. Non-starter for a product. | N/A |
| **`pf` (what we're doing)** | Kernel-level redirect of IP packets. Works for apps whose outbound IP actually goes through filtered interfaces — **which on modern macOS excludes a lot of locally-originated traffic** (we're literally seeing this: route-to gets us some things, not everything, and there's no principled fix). | Free, but intrinsically limited |
| **DYLD_INSERT / Frida** | Per-process injection. Blocked by SIP for signed apps. Doesn't scale. | N/A |

**Network Extension is the only path that truly "captures everything at OS level."** mitmproxy knew this — that's exactly why they shipped `mitmproxy-macos` as a Network Extension, and why mitmproxy on macOS requires it. pf alone is insufficient, even for them.

## Two realistic paths

**A. Bundle mitmproxy's already-approved Network Extension**

- They have a signed, notarized `Mitmproxy Redirector.app` shipped in their PyPI wheel
- Extract it, bundle it in our Electron app, talk to it from our Rust sidecar over a local socket
- We don't need our own Apple Developer account or entitlement approval
- Risk: mixed team-ID signing (their NE signed by their team, our shell signed by ours) — sometimes trips hardened runtime; needs careful code-signing attribute work
- Time: ~1 week of integration + testing

**B. Get our own Developer ID + ship our own NE**

- $99/yr Apple Developer fee
- File for NE entitlement from Apple — usually 1–3 weeks review, but they do approve "monitoring/capture" apps routinely
- Write a small Swift TransparentProxyProvider (~500 lines) that forwards flows over a Unix socket to our Rust sidecar, which keeps all the hudsucker MITM + event pipeline we already have
- Time: ~1–2 weeks of build work + Apple wait
- Clean, owns the whole stack, no external deps

## One more thing worth saying

Even with a Network Extension, **cert pinning still blocks TLS decryption** for apps that pin (ChatGPT.app, probably Claude.app, maybe Cursor for some hosts). NE can see the flow metadata and SNI but can't decrypt content that's pinned against us.

For pinned apps, the only scalable answer is reading the **session files those apps write to disk** — Claude Code writes to `~/.claude/sessions/`, opencode writes to `~/.local/share/opencode/`, Cursor writes chat logs, etc. These contain the full prompt/response text, already decrypted, persisted by the app itself. We watch them and ingest.

So the real capture architecture is layered:

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ macOS Network Extension (Transparent Proxy Provider)    │  every flow
│ → Rust sidecar MITM                                     │  including Bun
│ → Event stream + SQLite                                 │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                         +
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ File watcher on ~/.claude, ~/.local/share/opencode, ... │  pinned-app content
│ → Parse session JSON                                    │  when NE can't decrypt
│ → Same event stream                                     │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                         +
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ (Later) Browser extension for chatgpt.com, claude.ai,   │  web app content
│ midjourney.com, notion.so, canva.com                    │
│ → Same event stream                                     │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

The work we've already done — hudsucker MITM, CA lifecycle, event schema, SQLite store, React viewer — **stays intact**. We're replacing only the *ingress* (pf → NetworkExtension) and adding parallel collectors (file watchers, browser ext).

state.title: Find opencode session file layout

parts.text:
I'm finding a wealth of data from opencode — there's an active SQLite database, recent session files with diffs from today, log directories, and snapshot storage that I can work with.

Claude Code stores everything in `~/.claude/` with a 1.1 MB history file modified just this morning, plus session and project directories. Codex has a similar setup with its own history file and a massive 22 MB SQLite database of logs.

For the MVP file watcher, I should focus on the JSONL files since they're straightforward to parse — just tail the file and emit each new line as an event. The opencode session diffs and SQLite databases are more complex, so I'll start by examining what the JSONL formats actually contain to understand their structure.
Jackpot — lots of session data already on disk. Let me inspect the formats:

echo
echo
echo "=== opencode session_diff sample (most recent) ==="
latest=$(ls -t "$HOME/.local/share/opencode/storage/session_diff"/*.json 2>/dev/null | head -1)
echo "file: $latest"
echo "size: $(wc -c < "$latest") bytes"
head -c 2000 "$latest"
echo
echo
echo "=== opencode sqlite tables ==="
sqlite3 "$HOME/.local/share/opencode/opencode.db" ".tables" 2>&1 | head
echo
echo "=== sample rows from each opencode table (first 2 rows) ==="
for tbl in $(sqlite3 "$HOME/.local/share/opencode/opencode.db" ".tables" 2>&1); do
  echo "-- $tbl --"
  sqlite3 "$HOME/.local/share/opencode/opencode.db" ".schema $tbl" 2>/dev/null | head -5
  echo
done

state.title: Inspect Claude/Codex JSONL + opencode storage

parts.text:
Found it — opencode stores the complete AI interaction history in a SQLite database at `~/.local/share/opencode/opencode.db`, with separate tables for messages, message parts, sessions, events, and workspace metadata. This is the full record I need, not just request/response summaries.

Claude Code keeps user commands in `~/.claude/history.jsonl` but the actual conversations are in `~/.claude/sessions/` or project-specific session directories, while Codex has a similar split between `history.jsonl` (user messages only) and `logs_1.sqlite` (complete logs) plus `~/.codex/sessions/` for detailed session data.

For reliability, querying SQLite by monotonic ID or timestamp is far better than file watching — no race conditions, no parsing issues. My approach: on startup, find the max timestamp already seen in opencode.db, then poll every 1-2 seconds for new messages and emit SessionTurn events, storing everything locally in my own database.
This is a goldmine — opencode's SQLite has the full conversation log right there. Let me peek at what's actually in the `message` + `part` tables so I know what to parse:

echo "latest: $latest_proj"
if [ -n "$latest_proj" ]; then
  ls -la "$HOME/.claude/projects/$latest_proj" | head -10
fi

parts.text:
I found the opencode SQLite database structure—the `message` table stores conversation data as JSON blobs with metadata like role and model info, while the `part` table contains individual message components with types, tool calls, and their states. The database appears to be actively used.

parts.text:
The data is definitely there—240 messages coming through with the cursor at 0. My Rust code must not be entering the poll loop or it's failing silently somewhere. I'm thinking the WebSocket client connected successfully at that timestamp, but the broadcast channel might be getting closed before any subscribers can actually receive messages from it. Let me trace through the code logic more carefully to find where the disconnect is happening.

Actually, I think I've found the issue. The broadcast channel requires an active receiver to be listening before messages are sent, otherwise they just get dropped. Since the first poll tick fires immediately at startup before the subscriber connects, all 240 messages are probably being sent into an empty channel and discarded. The tokio broadcast design is "live subscription"—you have to be listening first, then you get new messages from that point forward. So `_rx0` stays alive on the stack, which means the channel always has at least one receiver and messages get buffered up to 1024. But here's the key issue: broadcast channels give each subscriber only messages sent *after* they subscribe, not the buffered history. The WS client connects at t=0.5s, but the source already fired all 1175 events at t=0, so they're stuck in `_rx0`'s queue and never reach the new subscriber. I need to either start the source after the client subscribes, delay the source, or implement message buffering.

The real problem is the source loops every 1500ms but after the first poll consumes all events, the cursor moves forward and subsequent polls find nothing new. For the MVP, the simplest fix is to set the initial cursor to something like "now - 5 seconds" on first run, so only new writes after startup flow through to subscribers.

For testing purposes, I could make this configurable with a flag like `--backfill-seconds` to control how far back to look on first run. The core issue is that broadcast channels only deliver to subscribers that exist at send time, so the test needs to ensure the subscriber is listening before the source starts emitting. Messages in the ring buffer BEFORE subscribe() are not seen.

Let me double-check the tokio broadcast docs though. They say new Receivers start at position 0 and emit all buffered messages, but the Sender::subscribe() docs clarify that new Receivers only see values sent *after* they're created. So subscribers definitely miss historical messages.

My approach for the MVP: on first run, initialize the cursor to the current max time_created in the database, so we only emit new events going forward. For testing, the user triggers a fresh opencode run, and we should see those new events come through.

For the broader capture goal, this same file-tailing approach works for claude-code's JSONL logs and codex's SQLite, but apps like ChatGPT and Claude that don't maintain local session files would still need the network interceptor or accessibility hacks. The network layer is still valuable for direct API usage and custom scripts that don't use session files, but for opencode specifically, we've found a much simpler path.

**This is the win.** 579 session entries captured — 60 minutes of our actual conversation with opencode, **with zero network interception, zero sudo, zero Network Extension, zero cert-pinning fights.**

## This changes the architecture

We don't need pf or a NetworkExtension to capture opencode — **opencode already writes the full conversation to a SQLite database on disk**, and we can tail it in 200 lines of Rust. Same goes for Claude Code (`~/.claude/projects/**/*.jsonl`) and Codex (`~/.codex/logs_1.sqlite`). For any AI CLI that persists its sessions locally, **file-tailing is strictly better than network MITM**:

| | Network MITM | File tail |
|---|---|---|
| Works across cert pinning | ❌ | ✅ |
| Works across Bun / custom HTTP stacks | ❌ | ✅ |
| Works offline (if app caches) | ❌ | ✅ |
| Needs sudo / pf / NE / CA trust | ✅ | ❌ |
| Gets structured data (role, model, tool-calls) | ❌ (raw JSON) | ✅ (already typed) |
| Needs per-tool parser | ❌ | ✅ |

Network interception is still valuable — for apps that **don't** persist sessions locally (raw Python/Node API scripts, browser extensions, etc.), and for capturing metadata like latency and token usage that file tails don't expose — but for the "big 3 CLIs" the file-watch path is dominant.

## Clean up your system + run the clean test

The pf rules, system proxy, dedicated `_reflex` user, and test CA from earlier are all still installed. Let's reset to zero and run with just the file watcher:

```bash
cd /Users/bhavya_gor/work/reflex.md

# 1. Stop everything
sudo pkill -f reflex-capture || true
pkill -f tail-events || true

# 2. Uninstall pf rules, system proxy, _reflex user, and the test CA
sudo bash scripts/install-hooks.sh --ca /tmp/reflex-live/reflex-ca.pem --uninstall
rm -rf /tmp/reflex-live /tmp/reflex-sidecar.log /tmp/reflex-events.log
sudo rm -rf /var/run/reflex-capture

# 3. Start the sidecar as your normal user, sources-only mode, no sudo
./rust/target/release/reflex-capture \
  --proxy-port 0 --ws-port 0 --transparent-port 0 \
  --sources opencode \
  --backfill-recent-minutes 120 \
  --data-dir ~/.reflex \
  > /tmp/reflex-sidecar.log 2>&1 &
disown

sleep 0.6
ws_port=$(head -1 /tmp/reflex-sidecar.log | node -e 'let d="";process.stdin.on("data",c=>d+=c);process.stdin.on("end",()=>console.log(JSON.parse(d).ws_port))')
echo "ws_port=$ws_port"

# 4. Start the tail in compact mode, filtering for real content
node scripts/tail-events.js --ws $ws_port 2>&1 | grep -E '(message|tool_call|reasoning)'
```

The last command will stream events **live** as you run new opencode commands — open another terminal, do `opencode run "hello"`, and you'll see the entire turn (user prompt, model name, assistant text, every tool call, every reasoning step) scroll by in real time.

parts.text:
I'm looking at the Claude Code JSONL schema structure now. User messages contain a role and content field where content can be either a string or an array with tool results, while assistant messages include the model name and a content array with different item types like thinking blocks, text responses, or tool use calls with their inputs.

Tool results appear as user-type messages with a content array containing tool use IDs and result data, and there are various other entry types like system metadata, permission modes, and file history snapshots. Each entry has common fields like a UUID, RFC3339 timestamp, session ID for grouping, parent UUID for threading, and environment details like working directory and git branch.

Now I'm designing the parser to handle each JSONL line by extracting the entry type, timestamp, session ID, UUID, and parent UUID...
